title: Why Kurdish militancy went into retreat
gist: Reviewing Aliza Marcus's 'Resurgence and Revolution', Hannah Lucinda Smith traces how the PKK built a quasi-state over a third of Syria via a backroom détente with Assad and a US alliance of convenience against ISIS, then destroyed much of that gain by relaunching its Turkish insurgency in 2015. With Turkish armed drones grinding it down, Assad toppled in December 2024 and Washington shown to be a transactional partner, Öcalan called on his fighters to disarm in 2025 — leaving open whether a movement that thrives in chaos and smuggling economies can function in stability.

insights.claim: The PKK today runs a quasi-state covering a third of Syria, has partnered with the US military against ISIS, and is one of the most globally recognisable fighting groups in the Middle East — a reversal from its early-2000s condition as a fractured, anachronistic remnant.
insights.speaker: Hannah Lucinda Smith
insights.so_what: A third of Syrian territory under a non-state actor's control is the baseline reality any Syrian reconstruction or energy investment thesis must contend with.
insights.quote: Today, however, the PKK and its regional franchises run a quasi-state covering a third of Syria
insights.locator: Today, however, the PKK and its regional franchises

insights.claim: The PKK used its 2000s ceasefire period as an opportunity to review tactics and hone fighting methods while simultaneously working to shift its international image, running a two-pronged strategy from its northern Iraq bases.
insights.speaker: Hannah Lucinda Smith
insights.so_what: A ceasefire by an insurgent group can be a capability-building period rather than de-escalation — a caution when reading the current 2025 peace process.
insights.quote: used the ceasefire period as an opportunity to review their tactics
insights.locator: Having retreated to its bases in northern Iraq

insights.claim: Attacks on civilian targets during the PKK's ceasefire period were claimed by front groups such as the 'Kurdish Freedom Hawks' or TAK, which were in fact directly controlled by the PKK.
insights.speaker: Hannah Lucinda Smith
insights.so_what: Attribution laundering via front groups means formal ceasefire compliance metrics understate actual violence — apply the same scepticism to the current process.
insights.locator: Attacks carried out on civilian targets in this period

insights.claim: After the 2004 Qamishli riots the PKK began sending seasoned fighters and trained ideologues into Syria to spread Öcalan's ideas and recruit Kurds politicised by Damascus's repression, building an underground network in the northeast seven years before the civil war erupted.
insights.speaker: Hannah Lucinda Smith
insights.so_what: The PKK's Syrian dominance was the product of a seven-year pre-positioning effort, not battlefield luck — a template for how patient non-state actors capture power vacuums.
insights.locator: After 2004, when Kurds in the Syrian city of Qamishli rioted

insights.claim: Rather than joining the armed uprising against Assad, the PKK arranged a backroom détente with the regime, which allowed it to emerge as a unified force while the mainly Arab rebel groups collapsed into extremism and infighting.
insights.speaker: Hannah Lucinda Smith
insights.so_what: Sitting out a civil war's opening phase can be the winning move — abstention preserved cohesion while committed factions destroyed each other.
insights.quote: Yet rather than taking on the regime by joining with the armed uprising, the PKK decided to arrange a backroom détente with Assad.
insights.locator: By the time the Syrian Civil War erupted

insights.claim: The ISIS assault on the YPG at Kobani in late 2014 was the turning point: a US already disillusioned with the Syrian rebel groups shifted support to the Kurds, starting with airstrikes and escalating into a full military alliance with American and British special forces on the ground.
insights.speaker: Hannah Lucinda Smith
insights.so_what: US partner selection in the Middle East is driven by battlefield convenience rather than ideological affinity — a pattern that repeats and expires.
insights.locator: When the black-flagged jihadis of ISIS turned their guns

insights.claim: Washington relied on Kurdish fighters as its ground troops to defeat ISIS precisely to avoid sending regular US forces into another Middle East war.
insights.speaker: Hannah Lucinda Smith
insights.so_what: The proxy-ground-force model is the default US approach to regional conflict, which makes local partners' survival contingent on continued American interest.
insights.locator: As Washington sought to push back and defeat ISIS

insights.claim: The YPG was rebranded as the Syrian Democratic Forces and brought Arab fighters into its ranks to legitimise US partnership, but the group's highest-ranking fighters remained PKK veterans and Rojava was turned into a quasi-state centred on Öcalan's ideas.
insights.speaker: Hannah Lucinda Smith
insights.so_what: The SDF's multi-ethnic branding is a façade over PKK command — relevant to how Ankara will treat any SDF integration into the new Syrian state.
insights.quote: That flimsy façade did little to hide the fact that the group’s highest-ranking fighters were all PKK veterans
insights.locator: In order to legitimise the partnership

insights.claim: Turkey's seizure of the Kurdish territory of Afrin in 2018 is identified as the moment the PKK realised the United States would be its ally only for as long as it suited American needs.
insights.speaker: Hannah Lucinda Smith
insights.so_what: A dated, concrete precedent for allied abandonment that other US partners will factor into their own hedging calculus.
insights.locator: Marcus pinpoints the Turks’ seizure of the Kurdish territory

insights.claim: Trump's reported plans to use Iranian Kurdish militias in his war against the regime in Tehran quickly fizzled once it became clear those fighters would not participate without American boots on the ground alongside them.
insights.speaker: Hannah Lucinda Smith
insights.so_what: The proxy-ground-force option against Iran is unavailable because prior abandonment destroyed the trust it requires — narrowing US options to direct force.
insights.locator: It seems unlikely that any Kurdish group will unquestioningly partner

insights.claim: ISIS was dislodged from Raqqa by 2017 and its caliphate was territorially finished by 2019, after which the US did little to prevent Erdoğan launching a series of cross-border offensives against the Kurdish quasi-state in Rojava.
insights.speaker: Hannah Lucinda Smith
insights.so_what: Partner value expires precisely when the mission succeeds — the structural trap of proxy warfare for the proxy.
insights.locator: By 2017, ISIS had been dislodged

insights.claim: Grown hubristic on Syrian successes, the PKK relaunched its insurgency in eastern Turkey after a ceasefire broke down in summer 2015, ordering teenage fighters in urban centres to build barricades and fire on Turkish security forces.
insights.speaker: Hannah Lucinda Smith
insights.so_what: Success in one theatre produced fatal overreach in another — a recurring pattern worth applying to other regional actors riding recent battlefield wins.
insights.locator: Even more problematically, the PKK grew hubristic

insights.claim: The Turkish state's response destroyed whole towns and city districts across the southeast and killed thousands, costing the PKK much of the Kurdish community support it had built through its Syrian campaign.
insights.speaker: Hannah Lucinda Smith
insights.so_what: Ankara's willingness to absorb heavy civilian destruction to crush insurgency sets the baseline for how it will respond to any renewed Kurdish autonomy push.
insights.locator: Inevitably, the Turkish state’s fightback was swift and brutal

insights.claim: The 2015 relaunch revealed a fundamental truth about the PKK: it had failed to recognise geopolitical realities or to think beyond armed struggle as a method.
insights.speaker: Hannah Lucinda Smith
insights.so_what: The group's strategic literacy is the binding constraint on the current peace process succeeding.
insights.quote: that the PKK had failed to recognise geopolitical realities, or to think beyond its methods of armed struggle

insights.claim: After 2020 Ankara escalated pressure on the PKK using homegrown armoured drone technology to strike the group in northern Iraq and, from 2021, in Syria as well.
insights.speaker: Hannah Lucinda Smith
insights.so_what: Indigenous Turkish armed drones materially shifted a decades-old insurgency balance — a live demonstration case underpinning Turkish drone export demand.
insights.quote: using its homegrown armoured drone technology to target the group in northern Iraq and, after 2021, also in Syria
insights.locator: After 2020, Ankara stepped up its pressure

insights.claim: Islamist rebels toppled Assad in December 2024, leaving the Kurds in Rojava more vulnerable to Turkish attack; their agreed integration into the new Syrian state has progressed slowly and been repeatedly knocked off course by outbreaks of fighting.
insights.speaker: Hannah Lucinda Smith
insights.so_what: Kurdish-Damascus integration is the unresolved variable determining whether northeast Syria stabilises enough for reconstruction capital to enter.
insights.locator: Meanwhile, in December 2024 Islamist rebels toppled Assad

insights.claim: In 2025, with few other avenues open, Öcalan called on PKK fighters to lay down their arms and the group entered new peace negotiations with Ankara.
insights.speaker: Hannah Lucinda Smith
insights.so_what: A durable Turkey-PKK settlement would remove a chronic domestic security drag on Turkish assets and reshape Ankara's Syria policy.
insights.locator: In 2025, with few other avenues left open

themes.theme: What kind of organisation the PKK actually is

insights.claim: Despite its apparent pivot to democracy and peaceful methods after the 2003 congress, the PKK never abandoned its willingness to use violence, its cult-like internal dynamics, or its unbending obedience to Öcalan.
insights.speaker: Hannah Lucinda Smith
insights.so_what: Institutional continuity beneath rebranding means the current disarmament call should be judged on verification, not declarations.
insights.quote: a group that, despite its apparent pivot towards democracy and peaceful methods, never abandoned its willingness to use violence, cult-like internal dynamics, and unbending obedience to Öcalan
insights.locator: The story she tells in deep and meticulously-sourced detail

insights.claim: The PKK is at its core a group that thrives in chaos — whether in porous borderlands where it controls and profits from smuggling, or in the ungoverned spaces of wartime Syria — and has yet to show it can be effective in times of stability.
insights.speaker: Hannah Lucinda Smith
insights.so_what: The organisation has a material stake in continued disorder, which is a structural argument against the durability of the 2025 peace process.
insights.quote: The PKK is also, at its core, a group that thrives in chaos, whether in porous borderlands where it controls and profits from smuggling, or in the ungoverned spaces of wartime Syria.
insights.locator: The PKK is also, at its core, a group that thrives in chaos

insights.claim: The PKK remains overly reliant on the ideas and directions of a leader who has spent the whole of this century in prison, with Öcalan unseen in person for nearly two decades and communicating only via delegations and lawyers visiting his island prison in the Sea of Marmara.
insights.speaker: Hannah Lucinda Smith
insights.so_what: Total dependence on one imprisoned leader makes the organisation's trajectory hostage to Turkish control of his communications — and to his mortality.
insights.locator: Öcalan, meanwhile, had become an Oz-like figure

insights.claim: The PKK has proved adept at morphing with the times, transforming from a leftist anti-imperialist force into an American battlefield ally, yet remains unsophisticated and far too optimistic about its prospects of international support.
insights.speaker: Hannah Lucinda Smith
insights.so_what: Ideological flexibility without strategic realism is the group's defining weakness — expect further misreadings of Western intent.

insights.claim: Much of the past decade's commentary on the PKK has been tainted by barely concealed enthusiasm for its ideology and methods, whereas Marcus's account draws mainly on former and often disillusioned PKK fighters.
insights.speaker: Hannah Lucinda Smith
insights.so_what: Western reporting on the Kurdish cause carries a systematic sympathetic bias — discount it when assessing the group's actual capabilities and intentions.
insights.quote: much of it tainted by barely concealed enthusiasm for its ideology and methods
insights.locator: That has brought a fresh rush of interest

insights.claim: Marcus ends optimistically on the renewed peace process, arguing that the same belief that drove the Kurdish fight for decades would now drive peace, for as long as Öcalan and the rebels believed in it.
insights.speaker: Hannah Lucinda Smith
insights.so_what: The peace case rests entirely on belief rather than institutional structure — a conditional forecast that inverts the moment Öcalan's position changes.
insights.quote: Belief drove the Kurdish fight for decades. Now it would drive peace, at least as long as Öcalan, and the rebels, believed in it,
insights.locator: Marcus ends on a note of optimism
